strengths: The paper targets a critical and timely challenge in diffusion- and flow-based online reinforcement learning: the prohibitive training and inference overhead caused by multi-step iterative sampling.

The methodological adaptations of MeanFlow models to maximum entropy RL are principled and well-derived. In particular, the introduction of the Average Divergence Network (ADN) for rapid likelihood estimation and the Effective Sample Size (ESS)-weighted dual-proposal SNIS estimator (AIVE) for policy improvement effectively resolve the core theoretical and practical bottlenecks.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple continuous control benchmarks (MuJoCo locomotion, DeepMind Control Suite, HumanoidBench, and AntMaze) shows competitive or superior return performance while cutting wall-clock training time roughly in half and operating with only 2 sampling steps.

Thorough ablation studies validate each individual component (MeanFlow vs. conditional flow matching, ADN vs. instantaneous divergence, the ESS dual-proposal weighting, and hyperparameter sensitivity).
weaknesses: The evaluation uses test-time Q-guided action selection (evaluating M=10 candidate actions and choosing the argmax Q), which provides a notable performance boost as shown in Figure 11(b). While some baselines also use action filtering, several others (such as DIME and FlowRL) are listed with N/A in Table 2, making it difficult to fully disentangle the gains from the MeanFlow representation versus test-time sample-and-rank optimization.

The method introduces noticeable algorithmic complexity during training: it requires training both an average velocity network and an average divergence network using Skilling–Hutchinson trace estimation, alongside a distributional critic and a two-proposal SNIS procedure evaluating 48 action samples per update step.
Minor presentation oversight: the abstract ends with an incomplete sentence ('Our code is available at ' with no link or anonymized repository specified).

strengths: Well-motivated approach targeting a major practical bottleneck of diffusion- and flow-based policies in online RL, namely the high computational overhead during training and multi-step inference.

Technically novel and mathematically sound framework: the introduction of the Average Divergence Network (ADN) ingeniously mirrors the MeanFlow average velocity concept to enable fast, single-step/few-step likelihood estimation without expensive numerical ODE integration.

The adaptive instantaneous velocity estimation strategy elegantly resolves the severe variance and sample degradation of standard Gaussian proposals at large ODE times by incorporating a policy proposal weighted dynamically via Effective Sample Size (ESS).

Extensive empirical validation across diverse and challenging continuous control benchmarks (MuJoCo locomotion, DeepMind Control Suite, and HumanoidBench), outperforming or matching prior diffusion-RL baselines with approximately 50% training time reduction and only T=2 sampling steps.

Thorough ablation studies verifying each component, including the necessity of ADN, MeanFlow formulation vs. standard flow matching, proposal weighting ratios, and multi-modal behavior learning on AntMaze.
weaknesses: The theoretical convergence results (Propositions B.1 and B.2) rely on strong idealizing assumptions (e.g., exact global minimizers, universal function expressivity, and infinite importance samples $K_1, K_2 \to \infty$), rendering them primarily conceptual sanity checks rather than deep theoretical guarantees.

Evaluation relies on test-time action selection (sampling $M=10$ candidate actions and picking the highest Q-value), which is a common heuristic in diffusion RL but partially offsets the inference efficiency gains of using $T=2$ steps compared to standard one-step policy architectures.

The method requires training two separate MeanFlow-like networks (the policy average velocity network and the average divergence network), adding implementation and tuning complexity despite the reported 5% time overhead of ADN.

strengths: Well-motivated integration of MeanFlow models into online MaxEnt RL: The paper addresses a known, major limitation of diffusion- and flow-based policies (high training and inference latency due to multi-step sampling) by adopting average velocity modeling to enable accurate few-step generation (T = 2).

Principled solutions to key technical bottlenecks: The paper introduces two clever techniques tailored to MeanFlow policies: (1) the Average Divergence Network (ADN), which circumvents expensive numerical Jacobian integration for log-likelihood estimation via Hutchinson trace estimation and a MeanFlow-style objective, and (2) Adaptive Instantaneous Velocity Estimation (AIVE), which combines two SNIS proposals adaptively weighted by their Effective Sample Size (ESS) to stabilize policy improvement across ODE time steps.

Comprehensive and rigorous empirical evaluation: The proposed MFPO is thoroughly evaluated across 5 MuJoCo locomotion environments, 6 hard DeepMind Control Suite tasks, and 3 high-dimensional HumanoidBench tasks against strong and contemporary diffusion/flow baselines (DIME, FlowRL, SAC-Flow, MaxEntDP, DACER, QVPO). MFPO demonstrates competitive or superior reward performance while reducing training wall-clock time by ~50% and achieving low inference latency.

Thorough ablations and diagnostic experiments: The paper provides insightful analyses, including the 2D multimodal toy visualization (Fig. 5), trajectory diversity analysis on AntMaze (Fig. 10), empirical ESS behavior across time (Fig. 1), and component-wise ablation studies (Table 3, Fig. 3, Fig. 11, Fig. 12).
weaknesses: Reliance on auxiliary training tricks and potential confounding factors: MFPO incorporates several orthogonal enhancements, such as distributional Q-learning (C51) and test-time action selection (selecting the best of M=10 candidate actions based on Q-values). As shown in Table 2, not all baselines share identical test-time action evaluation protocols (e.g., some baselines have N/A for candidate action selection), which complicates attributing pure algorithmic gains solely to the MeanFlow policy representation.

Theoretical convergence results are informal: Propositions B.1 and B.2 assume idealized conditions—such as exact global minimization of non-convex neural network losses, universal expressivity of the policy class containing the Boltzmann distribution, and asymptotic sample limits (K_1, K_2 -> infinity). While intuitive as conceptual sanity checks, they do not provide non-asymptotic or finite-sample convergence guarantees under function approximation.

Extra network parameterization: Approximating the action likelihood necessitates training an additional neural network (the Average Divergence Network), which increases architectural complexity and implementation overhead, even though the reported computational overhead during training is modest (~5%).
